stem: A dehydrated adult has plasma glucose 650 mg/dL, effective serum osmolality 315 mOsm/kg, beta-hydroxybutyrate 1.2 mmol/L, pH 7.36, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, and altered mental status. Which hyperglycemic crisis best fits this pattern?
rationale: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 define HHS by plasma glucose at least 600 mg/dL, hyperosmolarity (effective serum osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg or total osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg), absence of significant ketonemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate below 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones below 2+), and absence of significant acidosis (pH at least 7.3 and bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L). This client meets those HHS criteria, making B correct. DKA and mixed DKA-HHS require significant ketosis and metabolic acidosis, while euglycemic DKA does not fit the marked hyperglycemia and absence of DKA-level ketosis/acidosis.
educational_objective: Differentiate HHS from DKA and mixed DKA-HHS using current glucose, osmolality, ketone, pH, and bicarbonate criteria.
source_document_title: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16: Diabetes Care in the Hospital
source_locator: Table 16.1 Diagnostic criteria for DKA and HHS: HHS requires plasma glucose >=600 mg/dL; effective serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg or total serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg; beta-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones <2+; pH >=7.3 and bicarbonate >=15 mmol/L. All criteria must be met.
source_claim_supported: Marked hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with beta-hydroxybutyrate below 3 mmol/L and no significant acidosis meets current adult HHS diagnostic criteria rather than DKA or mixed DKA-HHS.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret diagnostic/laboratory findings, identify abnormalities, recognize complications, and monitor clients at risk for acute physiologic deterioration.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — hyperglycemic crisis laboratory interpretation

source_original.stem: A dehydrated client has a glucose level of 650 mg/dL, markedly elevated effective serum osmolality, and altered mental status. Which condition is most consistent with this pattern?
source_original.rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration from osmotic diuresis, often with neurologic changes. Option B is correct. The measured glucose and hyperosmolality exclude hypoglycemia and water intoxication, and fasting ketosis does not produce this extreme hyperglycemic hyperosmolar picture.
source_original.source_detail: HHS diagnostic criteria/clinical presentation: severe hyperglycemia (typically glucose >=600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration with minimal significant ketoacidosis; cognitive changes can accompany marked hyperosmolality. 2024 international consensus report, Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic/laboratory interpretation, postprocedure monitoring, device management and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Upgraded the primary source to ADA Standards of Care 2026, retained key B, and added ketone/pH/bicarbonate data so HHS is distinguished from DKA and mixed DKA-HHS using all current diagnostic domains. Replaced noncompetitive distractors with realistic hyperglycemic-crisis differentials and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current ADA Standards of Care 2026; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: ADA Standards 2026 Section 16 Table 16.1 Diagnostic criteria for DKA and HHS
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item includes all four HHS diagnostic domains and does not infer HHS from glucose/osmolality alone. Numeric criteria match the current ADA table.

distractor_audit.A: DKA requires significant ketosis and metabolic acidosis, absent here.
distractor_audit.B: Correct; all stated values meet current HHS criteria.
distractor_audit.C: Mixed DKA-HHS requires DKA-level ketonemia/acidosis in addition to hyperosmolarity, absent here.
distractor_audit.D: Euglycemic DKA is inconsistent with glucose 650 mg/dL and absent DKA-level ketosis/acidosis.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B satisfies all stated laboratory domains; adding ketone and acid-base values removes overlap with mixed DKA-HHS.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are recognized hyperglycemic-crisis diagnoses rather than unrelated metabolic conditions.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpretation of acute metabolic laboratory patterns.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked ADA 2026 Table 16.1, each numeric criterion, all four diagnoses, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing. B remained uniquely correct.
